intro: In this college you'll learn how to introduce yourself in Dutch: say your name, tell people where you come from, give your age and phone number, fill in a simple form, and greet your neighbours.

paragraphs.heading: Welcome — and why this matters
paragraphs.text: Welcome to the very first theme of your Dutch course: Wie ben je? — 'Who are you?'. Introducing yourself is the first thing you do in any language, and in the Netherlands you will do it again and again: at the gemeente, the town hall; at the doctor; at your children's school; and when you meet your neighbours. So although it feels basic, getting this right gives you confidence in every other situation, and it is the foundation for the whole inburgering exam. The two questions you will hear most often are Hoe heet je? and Wat is je naam? Both simply mean 'What is your name?'. You will also hear the polite version, Hoe heet u? Listen for that small word u — it is the respectful way to speak to someone you do not know yet. In this college I explain everything in English, but every Dutch word and every example sentence is spoken by a real Dutch voice, so you also train your ear and your pronunciation. Try to repeat each example out loud after you hear it — speaking from day one is the fastest way to learn. Are you ready? Laten we beginnen — let's begin.

paragraphs.heading: Saying your name: je or u?
paragraphs.text: To answer the question, you have three natural options. You can say Ik heet followed by your name, or Mijn naam is, or simply Ik ben. All three are correct and common: Ik heet Ayhan, Mijn naam is Ayhan, or Ik ben Ayhan. A quick pronunciation tip: the word mijn sounds a bit like the English word 'mine', because the Dutch letters ij are pronounced like 'eye'. Now, one of the most important ideas in Dutch is the difference between je and u. Je is informal: you use it with friends, family, children, and most people your own age. U is formal and polite: you use it with officials, with older people, and with anyone you want to show respect to. When you are not sure, start with u — it is never rude, and people will often invite you to switch to je. So to a friend you might ask En jij, hoe heet jij?, but to an official at the desk you would say En u, hoe heet u? The Dutch also tend to shake hands and say their own name when they meet someone new. This je-versus-u choice comes back in every single theme, so start noticing it right now.

examples.en: Nice to meet you, I'm Tom.

paragraphs.heading: Where are you from?
paragraphs.text: The next thing people ask is where you come from. The question is Waar kom je vandaan? — literally 'Where do you come from?'. You answer with Ik kom uit plus a country: Ik kom uit Turkije, Ik kom uit Syrië, or Ik kom uit Marokko. To say where you live now, use Ik woon in plus a city: Ik woon in Amsterdam. You can also state your nationality with Ik ben plus a nationality word, for example Ik ben Turks or Ik ben Syrisch. People often ask about language too: Welke talen spreek je? You answer with Ik spreek, for example Ik spreek Turks, Engels en een beetje Nederlands. That little phrase een beetje Nederlands — 'a little Dutch' — is one of the most useful things you can say in your first months: it signals people to speak slowly and to be patient with you. Notice the verb forms ik kom, ik woon, ik spreek. In Dutch the 'ik' form of most verbs is just the simple stem of the verb, so you can start making sentences very quickly. Practise saying where you come from and where you live until it comes out without thinking.

paragraphs.heading: Age, numbers and your phone number
paragraphs.text: Theme one also introduces numbers, because you need them for your age and your phone number. To ask someone's age you say Hoe oud ben je?, and you answer Ik ben plus a number plus jaar: Ik ben veertig jaar. Let's review the numbers from zero to ten: nul, een, twee, drie, vier, vijf, zes, zeven, acht, negen, tien. The tens are tien, twintig, dertig, veertig, vijftig. One thing surprises many learners: in Dutch you say the small number before the big one. So twenty-one is eenentwintig — literally 'one-and-twenty' — and thirty-five is vijfendertig. For a phone number the question is Wat is je telefoonnummer?, and you usually read the digits one by one, or in pairs. You will give your telefoonnummer constantly — at the doctor, at the gemeente, and in shops — so it is worth practising your own number out loud. And here is a small but powerful sentence for when someone speaks too fast: Kunt u dat herhalen? — 'Can you repeat that?'. Or you can ask Kunt u langzamer praten? — 'Can you speak more slowly?'. Never be afraid to use these; Dutch people will gladly slow down for you.

paragraphs.heading: Filling in a form
paragraphs.text: A very practical part of this theme is filling in a form — een formulier invullen. Forms are everywhere in the Netherlands, so you must recognise the standard fields. Voornaam is your first name and achternaam is your surname, your family name. Geboortedatum is your date of birth and geboorteplaats is your place of birth. Adres is your address, and it breaks into straat for street, huisnummer for house number, postcode for the postal code, and woonplaats for the town you live in. You will also see geslacht, meaning 'gender', with the words man and vrouw; nationaliteit, your 'nationality'; and often telefoonnummer and e-mailadres. Many official forms ask for your burgerservicenummer, the BSN — your personal citizen number — so keep it somewhere safe. At the bottom a form almost always asks for your handtekening, your signature, next to datum, the date. If a clerk hands you a form and you feel unsure, this one sentence saves the day: Kunt u mij helpen met dit formulier? — 'Can you help me with this form?'. Asking for help is completely normal and expected here, so use it whenever you need to.

examples.en: My date of birth is 12 May 1985.

examples.nl: Ik woon op de Kerkstraat, huisnummer 10.
examples.en: I live on Kerkstraat, house number 10.

examples.nl: Kunt u mij helpen met dit formulier?
examples.en: Can you help me with this form?

paragraphs.heading: Greetings & meeting your neighbour
paragraphs.text: Finally, let's put it together the way it really happens: greeting people. In the morning you say Goedemorgen, in the afternoon Goedemiddag, and in the evening Goedenavond. A simple Hallo or Hoi works any time with people you know. When you meet someone for the first time, say Aangenaam or Leuk je te ontmoeten — both mean 'nice to meet you'. To say goodbye, use Tot ziens, the casual Doei, or Tot morgen if you will see them tomorrow. Now imagine a new neighbour knocks on your door. You can say: Hallo, ik ben uw nieuwe buurman. Ik heet Ayhan. Aangenaam! For a woman it would be uw nieuwe buurvrouw. That one little introduction opens the door to your whole neighbourhood, and neighbours who know your name are neighbours who will help you. So practise this out loud today, together with your partner: greet each other, say your names, and ask where the other comes from. In the coming themes we build directly on these blocks — shopping, the weather, the doctor — but it all starts with a confident hello. Heel goed gedaan — well done — and I will see you in theme two!

examples.nl: Aangenaam, ik ben uw nieuwe buurman.
examples.en: Nice to meet you, I'm your new neighbour.
